Reader Submission What I learnt building a career at the intersection of compliance, AI, and research. Published : 14 October 2026. • Updated : 14 October 2026, 15:43. • CAMPUS. Mir Mohtasam Hossain Sizan. Design: Faisal Bin Iqbal. As a global financial compliance & crime associate at JPMorgan Chase, I investigate high-risk financial crime and file the reports that feed directly into federal law enforcement intelligence. It's demanding, detail-heavy work, and most days, it's invisible by design. A good investigation prevents a headline rather than making one. Alongside that career, I have spent the last several years publishing peer-reviewed research applying artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to financial crime detection, testing how far these methods can be pushed beyond what conventional rule-based compliance systems can see. Looking back, a few lessons stand out from that work, and I want to share them in case they're useful to anyone building a similar path. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source. Let AI-driven thinking guide your investigative work – and vice versa. Anti-money laundering (AML) compliance is fundamentally a pattern-recognition problem, and traditional AML systems are built on fixed rules: if a transaction matches a known pattern, it gets flagged. The limitation is obvious once you've worked in the field – rule-based systems only catch what they were already told to look for. That gap is what drove much of my research. One study I am particularly proud of built an unsupervised machine learning ensemble to detect new money-laundering typologies within transaction graphs – patterns a system trained only on known, labelled laundering behaviour would never catch, because they don't resemble anything it has seen before. That's close to the exact problem I evaluate in live investigations, where the most dangerous cases are often the ones that don't fit any existing template. I followed that work with related studies applying machine learning to credit card fraud detection and corporate bankruptcy prediction, and later to equity market forecasting using a hybrid ensemble model. In each case, I tested multiple algorithms – logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, and LightGBM – against real datasets rather than betting on one method. After all, in financial crime detection, a wrong model isn't an academic error; it's a missed case or a false accusation. My advice: don't treat your AML expertise and your AI research as separate skill sets. The strongest financial crime research comes from investigators who understand both the criminal behaviour and the modelling well enough to know where each one breaks down. Publish even when nobody is telling you to. Nobody required me to formalise my AML detection work into a peer-reviewed paper on emerging laundering typologies or to test ensemble AI models for fraud and market forecasting outside work hours. I did it because I wanted proof that the machine learning approach I trusted in live investigations would hold up to scrutiny from researchers with no stake in my day job. If you're wondering whether your AI-driven compliance work is "publication-worthy", my honest answer is you won't know until you write it up and submit it. Some of my early submissions were rejected. That's part of the process, not a sign to stop. title: K Bank recruits interns for job-linked program, all to complete AI tasks
excerpt: . [Digital Today reporter Ji-young Lee] K Bank has launched recruitment for a job-linked internship that will be evaluated mainly on artificial intelligence capabilities. The bank plans to assign all selected interns practical tasks such as building AI agents and improving work efficiency, and to offer regular employment opportunities to those who receive high evaluations. K Bank said on Wednesday it is starting recruitment for its "2027 first-half job-linked internship". The hiring is part of K Bank's strategy to secure "AI native" talent that it has pursued since the first half of this year. title: Should banks prepare for an 'agentic buy button''?
excerpt: Agentic Commerce. Should banks prepare for an 'agentic buy button''?. By John Adams. About John. twitter. johnhadams. mailto. john. adams@arizent. com. linkedin. john-adams-83444310. Published October 14, 2026, 4:17 p. m. EDT. |. Updated October 14, 2026, 5:00 p. m. EDT. 4 Min Read. Facebook. Twitter. LinkedIn. Email. Key insight : E-commerce risk technology concepts can also be used to protect agentic commerce payments, according to Visa. Forward look: The card brand argues agentic commerce standards should be interoperable. The world's largest payment companies have spent most of the past decade pushing a common payment experience for online and mobile app payments, an effort that could also help boost agentic commerce by standardizing all agentic payments. Processing Content. "We have seen huge value in standards," James Mirfin, Visa's senior vice president and global head of risk and security intelligence solutions, told American Banker. Mirfin spoke with American Banker ahead of publishing a Visa blog about agentic AI risks and how banks can respond. The blog is not a direct response to any specific security event or announcement, though it comes at nearly the same time that JPMorganChase warned about the risks inherent in accessing AI agents to perform banking tasks and amid Amazon's dispute with Meta over access to the social network's Muse AI assistant. "Bankers are spending a lot of time talking about AI security," Mirfin said. "Everyone is curious. ". Why worry?. The buzz over AI has been accompanied by often extreme worries about security, along with more plausible risks such as noncompliant AI agents. The risk isn't just fraud, but AI agents going outside their "instructions," or misinterpreting prompts, according to John Meyer, a managing director at Cornerstone Advisors. "If I set up an agent to buy a ticket when the fare falls under $500, what happens if it buys five tickets under $500?" Meyer told American Banker. "A lot of our clients are also worried about AI agents contributing to things like account takeovers. ". Tightening access controls can help address this risk, according to Meyer. "Many CIOs are looking at 'least privilege data access,'" Meyer said of the policy of strict limitations for AI agent authorization, such as dollar amounts or purchase parameters. This concept is partly borrowed from limits on traditional corporate spending cards that do not allow purchases outside of a particular merchant category or budget line item. Some of the AI fear from banks is also about responsibility for a bad transaction or increase of worry about hacking or a rogue AI agent, Meyer said, while noting it's important for banks to have a strategy to mitigate and respond to security breaches involving AI agents. Existing rules that govern responsibility for disputed card payments, such as Reg Z and Reg E, aren't clear about what happens in the case of a disputed agentic purchase, according to Meyer. Until regulatory clarity emerges, banks should make sure they have a policy for agentic payment disputes, and a strategy to battle and respond to fraud or scams involving AI agents, according to Meyer. Past as prologue. The answers to some of the concerns about agentic commerce security could be found in existing programs, according to Mirfin. "Agentic is similar to e-commerce," Mirfin said, adding measures that shield e-commerce from security risk while ensuring user experience can be adopted for agentic AI. As agentic commerce has expanded, standards are starting to emerge to guide transactions. "We have put our own standard out there, but many of these standards are designed to be agnostic," Mirfin said, adding it's important that these standards gain adoption and do not compete. "You don't want 50 competing approaches to this. ". Some of the steps to guide online and mobile payments can be used for agentic commerce, according to Mirfin. Charlotte’s Next Banking Revolution: What Happens When AI Meets Wall Street South?
excerpt: . Artificial intelligence is transforming how banks operate, make decisions, and serve customers. For Charlotte, one of America’s most important financial centers, the consequences could be enormous. By Alex Womack | Finance | October 14, 2026. For decades, Charlotte has built its economy around the movement of money. Banks, investment firms, insurance companies, and financial technology businesses have helped transform the Queen City from a regional commercial center into one of America’s most significant financial hubs. Now the industry faces another transformation. Artificial intelligence is beginning to change how loans are evaluated, how fraud is detected, how customers receive financial advice, and how thousands of banking employees perform their daily work. The implications go well beyond faster customer service. AI could fundamentally change the economics of banking—and Charlotte is positioned near the center of that transition. Charlotte Has an Enormous Stake in the Future of Finance. The Charlotte Regional Business Alliance estimates that approximately 104,000 people work in the region’s financial services sector , including more than 50,000 in banking. Major institutions such as Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Truist have established substantial operations in the city. Their presence supports a broader ecosystem of technology firms, professional services businesses, commercial real estate, universities, and startups. And the financial sector has long provided something especially valuable to the regional economy: high-paying professional careers. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Charlotte metropolitan area had approximately 116,000 jobs in business and financial operations occupations in May 2025, with an average annual wage of nearly $100,000. That occupational measure is broader than banking alone, but it illustrates how important knowledge-intensive professional work has become to the local economy. The next question is what happens when machines become capable of performing a growing share of that work. Bank of America Is Already Showing What AI Can Do. Charlotte-headquartered Bank of America provides one of the clearest examples of AI’s growing influence. The company introduced Erica, its virtual financial assistant, in 2018. What began as an automated banking assistant has evolved into a large-scale technology platform. According to the bank’s 2025 annual report, approximately 20 million customers used Erica nearly 200 million times during the fourth quarter of that year. But some of the most economically significant applications are happening behind the scenes. In July 2026, Bank of America announced expanded generative AI capabilities for EricaAssist, an internal tool used by more than 18,000 customer service employees. The system analyzes information during conversations, identifies relevant guidance, and assists representatives in answering customer questions. The bank reported that EricaAssist reduces average call times by nearly one minute. Consider the significance of that improvement across a large service operation. Even relatively small increases in productivity can become valuable when repeated across thousands of employees and millions of transactions. Importantly, Bank of America’s reported results are company-specific. They don’t establish that every financial institution can achieve the same savings. Nevertheless, they demonstrate that AI in banking is no longer a theoretical possibility. It is becoming part of the operating system. Wells Fargo Is Building AI Into Its Workforce. Wells Fargo, another major employer in Charlotte, describes a similarly ambitious transition. In its 2025 annual report, the company said approximately 190,000 employees had access to Microsoft Copilot Chat, while roughly 40,000 were using Microsoft 365 Copilot tools. title: Security Bank Expands AI Screening to Detect Potential Financial Crime
excerpt: Security Bank Corp. has expanded its financial crime screening coverage tenfold through an artificial intelligence (AI) system designed to identify potential matches against sanctions lists and other watchlists. The bank uses FinCense Screening, a platform developed by financial technology firm Tookitaki, to screen customers and their related contacts. The system can identify possible matches even when names have different spellings, word orders, or variations, addressing a challenge in the Philippines, where naming conventions can make exact-name matching less reliable. Traditional screening systems that depend heavily on identical name matches may overlook potential matches when names are spelled or arranged differently. By accounting for these variations, the AI-powered platform aims to improve the identification of individuals who may require further review. The system flags possible matches for human investigators rather than making final determinations. According to Security Bank’s head of financial crime compliance, Daniel Ang, the platform is scalable, helping it distinguish genuine matches from false positives, while being able to support transparent, auditable decisions. Security Bank said the upgrade extended screening to 100% of related contacts and significantly increased the number of confirmed matches identified each month. However, the bank did not disclose specific figures for these results. The project also received recognition at the Asian Technology Excellence Awards 2026, held on September 17, for its implementation of technology in retail banking. Stronger Safeguards Amid Regulatory Scrutiny. The upgrade comes as Philippine financial institutions continue strengthening their anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing safeguards. On February 21, 2025, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) removed the Philippines from its list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring, commonly known as the grey list. The decision followed the country's progress in addressing deficiencies in its anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing framework. The country is scheduled to undergo another mutual evaluation in 2027, according to the Philippine government's Administrative Order No. 46, issued in July 2026. The assessment will examine the country's compliance with international standards and the effectiveness of its safeguards against financial crime. What It Means for Customers. For ordinary depositors, the technology operates largely behind the scenes. More accurate name matching may help investigators identify potential risks while reducing false alerts involving people whose names resemble those on watchlists. However, a flagged match does not automatically mean that a customer has committed a crime. Human investigators must assess the available information before determining whether further action is warranted. Security Bank's expanded screening coverage reflects the growing role of AI in helping financial institutions strengthen compliance processes, identify potential risks, and make their reviews more efficient.

Deutsche Bank Deploys AI On-Premise in IB, Capital Markets
excerpt: From The Markets. Deutsche Bank Deploys AI On-Premise in IB, Capital Markets. 10. 14. 2026. On-premise deployment brings firm-specific AI into critical banking workflows while keeping data, institutional knowledge and activity within Deutsche Bank’s technology environment. Farsight , the platform helping global financial services firms become AI-native, announced its partnership with Deutsche Bank. Deutsche Bank has deployed Farsight at present across Investment Banking & Capital Markets teams in Europe and North America, bringing specialized AI directly into critical banking workflows while keeping sensitive data, proprietary knowledge and workflow activity within the bank’s own technology environment. The on-premise deployment enables Deutsche Bank teams to apply AI to internal data and workflows while maintaining greater control over how that information is accessed and used. Farsight can incorporate the bank’s prior work, internal standards and proprietary data into workflows tailored to how individual teams operate, including their preferred formats, processes and standards. Bankers can then generate and refine materials through an automated chat experience that incorporates context and feedback over time. “Our teams have very specific standards for what goes in front of a client, and those standards vary from group to group,” said George Tierney, Managing Director, Global Chief Operating Officer for M&A at Deutsche Bank. “Farsight gives our teams a way to apply AI to their own workflows and materials while operating within Deutsche Bank’s technology environment. That combination of control and customization is critical to making AI work in a global, regulated enterprise like Deutsche Bank. ”. Financial institutions are increasingly moving AI beyond standalone experimentation and general-purpose assistants to specialized workflows. For regulated firms, this shift depends on access to data, much of which is sensitive. Running Farsight within the bank’s infrastructure allows the platform to put that data to work where it can have the greatest impact, while financial institutions maintain control over the data. “Banks have spent decades building proprietary data, workflows and judgment that shape how their teams work,” said Samir Dutta, Co-Founder and CEO of Farsight. “Running Farsight within a bank’s own infrastructure allows that knowledge to remain inside the institution while becoming part of how teams use AI. By incorporating banker feedback, Farsight can help AI reflect how a bank approaches client work rather than relying solely on general-purpose outputs. ”. The Deutsche Bank deployment builds on Farsight’s growing presence across financial services, with the platform supporting teams at some of the world’s largest financial institutions. title: TBS & World Bank Group Co-Host Youth AI Summit in Bangkok
excerpt: Thailand. PR News. TBS & World Bank Group Co-Host Youth AI Summit in Bangkok. From AI Users to AI Producers: TBS joins global leaders to shape the future of jobs, artificial intelligence and the next generation. PUBLISHED : 14 Oct 2026 at 15:32. Share. Facebook. Reddit. BANGKOK, 12 October 2026 — Thammasat Business School (TBS) took the global stage at the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) in Bangkok, co-hosting a high-level youth event with the World Bank Group to explore the future of jobs, artificial intelligence and economic opportunities for the next generation. The event, titled “Jobs, AI, and the Next Generation,” brought together senior World Bank Group officials, distinguished academics and approximately 80 students from Thammasat Business School and other educational institutions in the region. Held as part of one of the world’s most significant international economic gatherings, the event provided a platform for young people to engage directly with global development leaders on the opportunities and challenges of an increasingly AI-driven economy. The collaboration highlighted TBS’s growing international engagement and its commitment to connecting students with global expertise, influential decision-makers and real-world challenges that extend far beyond the classroom. From AI Users to AI Producers. A central message of the event was the need to rethink how universities prepare graduates for an economy increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. Associate Professor Dr Surat Teerakapibal, Dean of Thammasat Business School, emphasised that universities must move beyond teaching students how to use AI technologies and instead empower them to create new value through innovation. “Our graduates must not only know how to use AI; they must be able to create AI-powered solutions and become producers of AI-driven innovation. At Thammasat Business School, we are committed to developing future business leaders who do not simply adapt to technological change, but actively shape it,” said Dean Surat. This vision reflects a fundamental shift in business education. As AI tools become increasingly accessible, the competitive advantage of future graduates will depend not simply on their ability to use existing technologies, but on their capacity to develop innovative applications, solve complex business problems and create new economic opportunities. For TBS, becoming an AI producer does not necessarily mean that every graduate must become a programmer or technology specialist. Rather, it means developing the ability to combine business knowledge, creativity and technological understanding to design AI-enabled solutions, develop new business models and drive organisational transformation. The message underscores the importance of preparing graduates not only for the jobs of tomorrow, but also to become creators of entirely new opportunities. Connecting the Next Generation with Global Leaders. The event featured a distinguished line-up of international development leaders and academics, reflecting the importance of collaboration between global institutions and higher education. Roya Rahmani, Director for Global Engagement at the World Bank Group, delivered the welcoming remarks, followed by an address from Dean Surat. The main discussion brought together Mahesh Uttamchandani, the World Bank Group’s Regional Practice Director for Digital and AI, and Professor Dr Pavida Pananond, Professor of International Business at Thammasat Business School. Moderated by Siratthaya “Fern” Isarabhakdi, founder of Wealth Me Up and anchor at The Standard Wealth, the conversation explored how AI is reshaping employment, business competitiveness and economic opportunities, particularly for young people in developing economies. title: Human in the loop or human clicks “approve”?
excerpt: . We often treat human oversight as the safety net for AI. Let the AI prepare the recommendation and propose the action, and then put a human in the loop to approve it. Problem solved. Except there is one uncomfortable question:. What happens when the human stops reviewing and just starts clicking?. As AI agents take more actions, the number of decisions requiring human approval can grow quickly. A person who receives one unusual request may examine it carefully. A person who receives hundreds of similar requests every day may not. At some point, “human in the loop” can become human just clicking approve. Human oversight is not automatically meaningful oversight. The assumption sounds reasonable: humans provide judgement, context, and accountability that AI lacks. But simply adding a person to a workflow does not guarantee any of those things. NIST has cautioned against assuming that a human overseer will automatically provide effective governance. Human decision-makers bring their own cognitive biases, and the effectiveness of different human-AI configurations depends heavily on how roles and responsibilities are designed. Research also shows how easily people can over-rely on automated recommendations. In one experiment involving 292 participants, people followed algorithmic recommendations more closely than equivalent human recommendations. More importantly, when participants were able to monitor and adjust the automated recommendation, they were less likely to intervene when the algorithm made its largest errors. The researchers concluded that adding a human in the loop increased uptake of automation while decreasing decision accuracy in their experiment. That is automation bias: the tendency to rely too heavily on automated output. The EU AI Act explicitly recognizes this risk. For high-risk AI systems, Article 14 says people responsible for human oversight should be able to understand system limitations, correctly interpret outputs, override or reverse them, and remain aware of the tendency to over-rely on AI-generated recommendations. In other words, the regulator does not consider the mere presence of a human sufficient. The human must actually be capable of challenging the system. In this sense, approval does not always mean a judgement has been made. Imagine an AI agent handling procurement. Most transactions are routine. The agent prepares an action and asks an employee to approve it. Approve. Approve. Approve. Approve. After hundreds of correct recommendations, another approval appears. How carefully does the employee review number 237?. This problem becomes even harder with autonomous agents. A traditional application may require occasional approval. An agent can potentially perform hundreds or thousands of actions as it works toward a goal. OpenID contributors have raised precisely this scalability concern: per-action approval can lead to consent fatigue and reflexive approval, undermining the control it was supposed to provide. So perhaps the question should not be on where we can insert human approval, but where does human judgement genuinely add value? Maybe humans should manage boundaries, not clicks. Meaningful human oversight may require a different model. Instead of asking people to approve every routine action, organizations can define in advance what the agent is allowed to do independently and what requires escalation. For example:. An agent may process standard transactions below a certain risk threshold. But an unusual payment, policy exception, sensitive data access, or action above a defined financial threshold may require human review. The human then focuses attention where judgement matters rather than becoming a bottleneck for thousands of predictable decisions. NIST’s recent work on post-deployment AI monitoring identifies scaling human-driven monitoring as an open challenge and asks how oversight should vary according to risk and use case.
